questions.prompt: Ich sehe ___ Hund.
questions.explanation: The direct object is accusative masculine, so der changes to den.

questions.prompt: Wir kaufen ___ Apfel.
questions.explanation: The direct object is accusative masculine, so the article is den.

questions.prompt: Ich gebe ___ Kind ein Buch.
questions.explanation: The recipient is a dative neuter noun, so das changes to dem.

questions.prompt: Sie hilft ___ Frau.
questions.explanation: helfen governs the dative; feminine die becomes der in the dative.

questions.prompt: Das Geschenk ist für ___.
questions.explanation: für governs the accusative, so the first-person pronoun is mich.

questions.prompt: Kommst du mit ___?
questions.explanation: mit governs the dative, so the first-person pronoun is mir.

questions.prompt: Wir fahren ___ Berlin.
questions.explanation: With a city name and no article, movement to Berlin normally uses nach.

questions.prompt: Ich bin ___ Hause.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression zu Hause means “at home,” so zu is the correct preposition here.

questions.prompt: Sie geht ___ Schule.
questions.explanation: Movement into the school as a destination uses the accusative phrase in die Schule.

questions.prompt: Wir sind ___ Bahnhof.
questions.explanation: am is the contraction of an dem and is commonly used for a location at the station.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly negates “Ich habe ein Auto”?
questions.explanation: kein negates an indefinite noun phrase, so ein Auto becomes kein Auto.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly negates “Ich komme heute”?
questions.explanation: nicht negates the adverbial or verbal statement here and normally follows the time phrase.

questions.prompt: Which form is the negative article for feminine singular?
questions.explanation: The feminine nominative and accusative negative article is keine.

questions.prompt: Which modal verb means “can / be able to”?
questions.explanation: können expresses ability or possibility.

questions.prompt: Which modal verb means “must / have to”?
questions.explanation: müssen expresses necessity or obligation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a modal verb correctly?
questions.explanation: A modal verb is conjugated and the second verb remains an infinitive at the end: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means “You may sit down” formally?
questions.explanation: dürfen expresses permission, and the formal subject Sie takes dürfen.

questions.prompt: Which is the normal statement order?
questions.explanation: In a German main-clause statement, the finite verb is normally in second position; Heute occupies the first position and arbeite follows.

questions.prompt: Which is the normal yes/no question?
questions.explanation: A yes/no question normally puts the finite verb first: Kommst du heute?

questions.prompt: Which is the normal W-question?
questions.explanation: A W-question begins with the question word, followed by the finite verb and subject.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly places a separable prefix?
questions.explanation: In a simple main clause, the finite verb is second and the separable prefix moves to the end.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly places the infinitive after a modal?
questions.explanation: With a modal in a main clause, the infinitive normally goes to the end.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly places nicht in “I do not live in Berlin”?
questions.explanation: The sentence-level negator nicht follows the finite verb and normally precedes the final phrase being negated.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the correct formal question “Where do you live?”
questions.explanation: The formal pronoun Sie follows the finite verb in a W-question: Wo wohnen Sie?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a correct command to one person?
questions.explanation: The informal singular imperative of kommen is Komm; bitte softens the command.

questions.prompt: The German infinitive usually ends in -en.
questions.explanation: Most regular German infinitives end in -en, although a small number end in -n, such as sein.

questions.prompt: The finite verb is normally in second position in a German main-clause statement.
questions.explanation: German main clauses normally use verb-second order, even when another element such as Heute begins the sentence.

questions.prompt: The accusative marks the direct object.
questions.explanation: The direct object is commonly marked by the accusative case, which is especially visible in masculine articles.

questions.prompt: The dative is commonly used for a recipient or indirect object.
questions.explanation: A recipient such as dem Kind in Ich gebe dem Kind ein Buch is marked with the dative.

questions.prompt: German articles never change with case.
questions.explanation: Articles change with gender, number and case: der can become den, dem or des.

questions.prompt: kein negates a noun phrase without a definite article.
questions.explanation: kein behaves like an indefinite article and negates nouns such as ein Auto or bare nouns.

questions.prompt: A modal verb normally sends the second verb to the end of a main clause.
questions.explanation: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen places the infinitive sprechen at the end.

questions.prompt: All German nouns have grammatical gender that always matches biological sex.
questions.explanation: Grammatical gender is a noun-class property; it often differs from natural gender and must be learned.
